# Education in Poland
Education in Poland begins typically at age six or seven with primary school (szkoła podstawowa), which currently lasts eight years following a reform in 2017 that abolished the three-year junior high school (gimnazjum) system. Prior to this, the system consisted of six years of primary school followed by three years of gimnazjum. Compulsory education generally ends at age 18 after completing upper secondary education, which includes general secondary schools (liceum) lasting four years and culminating in the "Matura" exam that qualifies students for higher education.
Vocational and technical education is provided by technical schools (technikum) and basic vocational schools (zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa). Technical schools offer five-year programs that combine vocational training with the Matura exam, preparing students for trades such as accounting, mechanics, and electronics. Basic vocational schools offer three years of training leading to a certificate, with opportunities to pursue the Matura via additional schooling. At the tertiary level, Poland follows the Bologna process, offering three-year bachelor's degrees followed by two-year master's degrees, with some long-cycle degrees (up to six years) in fields like medicine. Doctoral studies typically take about three years. University grading uses a scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (excellent), with increments of 0.5 points.
